html:
A sandstone cliff about 150 km long in central Mali, home of the Dogon people, who settled there from about the 14th and 15th centuries, below the older cave dwellings of the Tellem.

The Dogon built villages of mud houses and granaries against the rock, and kept their own religion of ancestors and spirits, with mask dances and the Sigi ceremony held about every sixty years. French anthropologists made them famous in the 20th century, and their masks are prized in African art. UNESCO listed the site in 1989. Since 2015 violence between Dogon militias and Fula herders, fed by the Mali War, has killed hundreds.
